The routine post-opening inspection cycle is out of this model. D1 covers plan check and construction inspections only; San Diego's risk-based routine inspection frequency is asserted in notes.md from other sources but no primary document stating it was captured.
The county's internal criteria for accepting a plan as 'complete' cannot be verified against the reasonable-person list D7 publishes — the same gap as LA County's.

Mobile food facilities are out of scope here (San Diego runs a separate MFF track with its own construction guide, operations FAQ — currently 'Removed for pending updates' per D3 — and template submittal packages). A separate gold model would be needed.

Cottage Food Operations are explicitly a non-plan-check track ('must obtain a permit or registration from FHD, but are not required to submit plans'), as are public pools, body art and some massage establishments handled by the same unit. These are the disentanglement boundaries for this task.
No observed tier at all: San Diego publishes an inspection-results search but no permit-volume or cycle-time dataset was captured, so gold_tier is 'designed' rather than 'designed+observed'.

D1 references a 'Plan Check Flow Chart' on its own page 10 and a 'Food Facility Final Inspection Checklist' on page 11; the diagrammatic page is an image in the extracted text (D2 is the standalone version of the same chart), and the final-inspection checklist body was not quoted here.
notes:
Why a third food_facility model: San Diego completes a three-county natural experiment on one statute. The California Retail Food Code gives all three counties the same thin skeleton — plans before construction, a 20-working-day clock, a permit required to open, grading left to local option — and the three designed visibly different machines. SF folds DPH review inside a single DBI Permit Center submittal as a routing station; LA takes a direct EH submittal and deliberately sequences its final inspection AFTER all city Building & Safety approvals; San Diego takes a direct Accela submittal, requires its own approval BEFORE a building permit may issue (HSC 114380(e)), and then requires building/fire final approval before its own final inspection — i.e. it gates both ends. Scoring the same solver across all three isolates local design from statutory mandate.

San Diego is the most operationally explicit of the three, and consequently has only three staff_only activities: the demand-driven rationing of review and inspection lead times (A09), the one-year retention rule on inspected plan sets (A14), and the continuity-of-reviewer policy buried in a flow-chart footnote (A27). The same pattern holds as in LA County — the more a county publishes about its procedure, the less of its hidden layer is sequence and the more it is capacity, records and staffing. That is a finding about where opacity actually lives in these processes, not an artifact of document supply.

Three details worth singling out. (1) San Diego charges on both sides of every correction loop: each plan resubmittal is invoiced and must be paid before it is looked at, and each construction inspection past the third is invoiced too — so the cost of a rework round is explicit and double, where LA says only that 'additional fees apply' and SF publishes no plan-review amount at all. (2) The express lane is priced as a bare 2x multiplier with no turnaround promise attached; LA sells the same thing at roughly 1.5x with a published 10-business-day ceiling. Same statutory silence, two different ways to monetise the queue. (3) D7, San Diego's AB 671 FAQ, is near-verbatim identical to LA County's independently published FAQ — same 'complete plan' list, same resubmittal-vs-change-of-scope split, same worked examples down to 'Relocating or resizing a sink, floor sink, or floor drain per correction comments' and 'Adding equipment requiring referral to other agencies (CDFA, FDA, USDA)'. Two counties converging word-for-word on a taxonomy that appears nowhere in HSC 114380(f) is either shared CDPH/CCDEH guidance behind the scenes or an obvious reading of the statute, and the public record cannot distinguish the two. Whichever it is, it means the 'local design' in this seam may be a single design adopted twice — a caution for any metric that treats the two counties as independent observations.
